claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings presented in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Ca2+ signals produced in the PC dendrite by climbing fiber excitation are a biochemical trigger for inducing synaptic plasticity.
claims.source: Ca2+ signals produced in the PC dendrite by climbing fiber excitation have been subject to intensive investigation because intracellular Ca2+ elevation is a biochemical trigger for inducing synaptic plasticity (Finch et al., 2012; Lamont and Weber, 2012), and synaptic plasticity has been implicated as a neural correlate of motor learning and memory (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Ito and Kano, 1982).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Finch et al., 2012; Lamont and Weber, 2012; Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Ito and Kano, 1982).

claims.claim: When activated alone, climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signals are insufficient to induce synaptic re-weighting of parallel fiber-PC synapses.
claims.source: When activated alone, climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signals are insufficient to induce synaptic re-weighting of parallel fiber-PC synapses.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about cerebellar plasticity mechanisms.

claims.claim: Amplification of climbing fiber signals by preceding parallel fiber activity can achieve a threshold level of Ca2+ elevation necessary to generate short- and long-term plasticity at parallel fiber inputs.
claims.source: However, amplification of climbing fiber signals by preceding parallel fiber activity can achieve a threshold level of Ca2+ elevation necessary to generate short- and long-term plasticity at parallel fiber inputs (Wang et al., 2000; Brenowitz and Regehr, 2005; Tanaka et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Wang et al., 2000; Brenowitz and Regehr, 2005; Tanaka et al., 2007).

claims.claim: By preventing parallel fiber enhancement of Ca2+ signaling, MLI-mediated inhibition may suppress the induction of climbing fiber-mediated plasticity despite the interaction of these two inputs.
claims.source: Therefore, by preventing parallel fiber enhancement of Ca2+ signaling, MLI-mediated inhibition may suppress the induction of climbing fiber-mediated plasticity despite the interaction of these two inputs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental findings of the study.

claims.claim: Genetic deletion of GABAARs from PCs impedes consolidation of motor learning.
claims.source: Interestingly, genetic deletion of GABAARs from PCs impedes consolidation of motor learning (Wulff et al., 2009), a result that may be attributable to the disinhibition of PCs and indiscriminate plasticity produced by unregulated, supralinear climbing fiber Ca2+ signaling.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Wulff et al., 2009) and inference about the mechanism.

claims.claim: Interneurons in the cortex, hippocampus, amygdala, and striatum dynamically regulate dendritic processing in their postsynaptic targets.
claims.source: Interneurons in the cortex, hippocampus, amygdala, and striatum are known to dynamically regulate dendritic processing in their postsynaptic targets, electrogenically gating synaptic interactions that lead to alterations in circuit function (Paulsen and Moser, 1998; Letzkus et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Paulsen and Moser, 1998; Letzkus et al., 2015).

claims.claim: During behavior, MLIs exert a widespread suppression of supralinear climbing fiber Ca2+ signaling throughout the PC dendrite.
claims.source: Although inhibition can elicit branch-and synapse-specific control of Ca2+ signaling (Callaway et al., 1995; Chiu et al., 2013), our results indicate that during behavior, MLIs exert a widespread suppression of supralinear climbing fiber Ca2+ signaling throughout the PC dendrite, perhaps owing to the highly coherent activation of their ensemble during orofacial movements (Astorga et al., 2017; Gaffield and Christie, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion of the study supported by experimental data and citations to prior work (Callaway et al., 1995; Chiu et al., 2013; Astorga et al., 2017; Gaffield and Christie, 2017).

claims.claim: Ca2+ responses in PC dendrites are not always augmented by the context of active motor behavior.
claims.source: A novel aspect of our findings is that Ca2+ responses in PC dendrites are not always augmented by the context of active motor behavior.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging.

claims.claim: Climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ activity increases in PCs at the onset of water consumption.
claims.source: During these trials, as well as during un-cued licking with free access to water, climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ activity increases in PCs at the onset of water consumption (Gaffield et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Gaffield et al., 2016).

claims.claim: External sensory cues that can guide associative learning evoke graded climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signals in PC dendrites.
claims.source: This hypothesis is consistent with work showing that external sensory cues that can guide associative learning (e.g., classical eyeblink conditioning), evoke graded climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signals in PC dendrites (Najafi et al., 2014a; Najafi et al., 2014b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Najafi et al., 2014a; Najafi et al., 2014b).

claims.claim: Spike bursting of granule cells could shift the balance of parallel fiber excitation and feed-forward inhibition through short-term plasticity.
claims.source: Spike bursting of granule cells could shift the balance of parallel fiber excitation and feed-forward inhibition through short-term plasticity (Häusser and Clark, 1997; Grangeray-Vilmint et al., 2018), perhaps unlocking the ability of parallel fibers to generate non-linear Ca2+ signaling in PCs when activated by multimodal streams of sensorimotor information, as occurs during associative learning (Chadderton et al., 2004; Ishikawa et al., 2015; Giovannucci et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to prior work (Häusser and Clark, 1997; Grangeray-Vilmint et al., 2018; Chadderton et al., 2004; Ishikawa et al., 2015; Giovannucci et al., 2017).

claims.claim: MLIs inhibit one another through their structured GABAergic interconnections.
claims.source: In addition, MLIs inhibit one another through their structured GABAergic interconnections (Kim et al., 2014; Rieubland et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kim et al., 2014; Rieubland et al., 2014).

claims.claim: By gating supralinear climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signaling, molecular layer inhibition may prevent unwarranted or unnecessary adaptation during accurately performed movements.
claims.source: By gating supralinear climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signaling, molecular layer inhibition may prevent unwarranted or unnecessary adaptation during accurately performed movements.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study inferred from the experimental findings.

results.result: Prior work establishes that motor learning in the cerebellar cortex involves climbing fiber instruction of synaptic modifications at parallel fiber-PC synapses through supralinear Ca2+ signaling that triggers long-term depression (LTD).
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C8, C9, and C10 are all supported by citations to established prior work and represent the foundational knowledge upon which the current study is built. These claims accurately summarize the prevailing model of cerebellar motor learning.

results.result: Prior work establishes that climbing fibers fire continuously at 1-2 Hz, PCs receive sensorimotor information from parallel fibers during movements, and MLIs provide feed-forward inhibition that can attenuate parallel fiber EPSPs and reduce climbing fiber-evoked responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C11, C12, C13, and C14 are all supported by citations to prior work and establish the relevant background about cerebellar circuit activity and MLI function. These claims accurately represent established knowledge in the field.

results.result: During practiced licking movements in awake mice, climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signals in PC dendrites showed no enhancement compared to spontaneous events during quiescence, despite parallel fiber and MLI co-activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C15, C22, and C25 are supported by in vivo Ca2+ imaging data (Figure 1D, 1G). The statistical analysis shows no significant difference in Ca2+ event amplitudes between licking and non-licking states (p=0.99), and no covariation with MLI activity. The use of GCaMP6f is validated by C23.

results.result: Chemogenetic suppression of MLI activity using hM4d enhanced climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signals in PC dendrites specifically during licking movements when MLIs are normally active, but not during quiescence.
results.evaluation: Claims C16, C26, C27, and C28 are supported by in vivo imaging with chemogenetic manipulations (Figure 2C-F). The effect was conditional on behavior, occurred only in hM4d-expressing mice, and was statistically significant. Control experiments (C28) rule out off-target CNO effects.

results.result: Chemogenetic suppression of MLI activity did not affect the rate of Ca2+ events in PCs or significantly alter licking dynamics when hM4d expression was limited to unilateral Crus II.
results.evaluation: Claims C29 and C31 are supported by experimental data showing no significant effect on Ca2+ event rates (p=0.51, Figure 2G) or licking behavior (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). This controls for potential confounds from altered motor output or climbing fiber firing rates.

results.result: MLI activity suppression enhanced Ca2+ signaling in the majority of PC dendrites (~70% of dendrites, ~66% of dendritic area) with a modest decrease in inter-branch variability during licking.
results.evaluation: Claims C32, C33, and C34 are supported by quantitative analysis of in vivo imaging data (Figure 3B, C, G, H). ROC analysis and statistical tests support the widespread effect of MLI disinhibition, though the reduction in inter-branch variability was modest.

results.result: Direct imaging of climbing fibers showed regular Ca2+ events at rates comparable to PC dendrites, increased frequency at licking onset, but no difference in event amplitudes between licking and non-licking states or with MLI activity suppression.
results.evaluation: Claims C35, C36, C37, and C38 are supported by in vivo imaging of climbing fibers expressing GCaMP6f (Figure 4B-G). Statistical tests show no significant differences in amplitudes (p=0.89 for behavior, p=0.66 for CNO), ruling out presynaptic changes as the mechanism for enhanced PC Ca2+ signals.

results.result: In acute slices, brief parallel fiber stimulation paired with climbing fiber activation produced linear summation of Ca2+ responses, but optogenetic suppression of MLI feed-forward inhibition revealed supralinear Ca2+ signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C40, C41, and C42 are supported by ex vivo slice recordings with optogenetic manipulations (Figure 5B-D). Statistical tests show linear summation in control (100.5±2.1%, p=0.78) but supralinearity with disinhibition (109.9±2.4%, p=0.0003). GtACR2 efficacy was validated against pharmacological GABA blockade (C40).

results.result: The enhancement of climbing fiber Ca2+ signaling by parallel fibers in the absence of MLI inhibition was timing-dependent and did not affect somatic complex spike spikelets.
results.evaluation: Claims C43 and C44 are supported by slice recording data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, Figure 5F). The timing dependence and compartmentalized effect on dendrites versus soma are consistent with dendritic mechanisms of supralinearity.

results.result: Prolonged parallel fiber stimulation (9 vs 3 stimuli) overcame MLI feed-forward inhibition to produce supralinear climbing fiber Ca2+ signals in the majority of PC dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claims C45, C46, and C55 are supported by slice recording data (Figure 6B-D). Statistical comparison shows significant supralinearity with 9 stimuli (114.7±3.6%, p=0.005) but not with 3 stimuli, demonstrating activity-dependent recovery of supralinearity.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of MLIs during prolonged parallel fiber stimulation abolished supralinear Ca2+ signaling in PC dendrites in a graded manner dependent on MLI activity level.
results.evaluation: Claims C47 and C48 are supported by slice recordings with bidirectional optogenetic manipulation using bReaChES (Figure 6E-G). Statistical tests show abolition of supralinearity (121.5±5.3% to 98.0±3.5%, p=0.004) and graded effects with varying light intensity.

results.result: The balance of parallel fiber excitation and MLI-mediated feed-forward inhibition regulates climbing fiber Ca2+ signaling in PC dendrites, with MLIs suppressing supralinearity during brief parallel fiber activation but allowing recovery with prolonged activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C6, C7, C17, and C18 represent the central findings integrating both in vivo and ex vivo results. The claims are supported by converging evidence from chemogenetic (Figures 2-3) and optogenetic (Figures 5-6) manipulations showing bidirectional control of supralinearity by MLI activity.

results.result: During practiced movements, MLIs enforce normalization of climbing fiber Ca2+ signals in PC dendrites by preventing parallel fiber enhancement through feed-forward inhibition that attenuates parallel fiber EPSPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C49 and C50 are primary conclusions supported by the integration of in vivo imaging (showing no enhancement during behavior) and ex vivo recordings (showing MLI-mediated suppression of supralinearity). The mechanistic explanation is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Prior work establishes that parallel fibers drive PC simple spiking with MLI modulation, climbing fibers produce dendritic Ca2+ spikes subject to parallel fiber amplification, and parallel fiber EPSPs inactivate K+ currents to facilitate climbing fiber Ca2+ spike propagation.
results.evaluation: Claims C51, C52, and C53 are supported by citations to prior work and provide mechanistic context for interpreting the current findings. These claims accurately represent established knowledge about PC dendritic physiology.

results.result: Climbing fiber Ca2+ signals trigger synaptic plasticity, with supralinear enhancement by parallel fibers achieving the threshold for LTD induction; MLI-mediated inhibition may suppress plasticity by preventing this enhancement.
results.evaluation: Claims C56, C57, and C58 are supported by citations to prior work establishing the role of Ca2+ in plasticity. Claim C59 is a reasonable inference from the current findings, though direct plasticity measurements were not performed in this study.

results.result: Genetic deletion of GABAARs from PCs impedes motor learning consolidation, consistent with a role for MLI-mediated inhibition in preventing indiscriminate plasticity; MLIs exert widespread suppression of supralinear Ca2+ signaling throughout PC dendrites during behavior.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is supported by citation to prior work with mechanistic interpretation. Claims C61 and C62 integrate prior knowledge about interneuron function with the current findings showing widespread MLI effects on PC Ca2+ signaling during behavior.

results.result: Ca2+ responses in PC dendrites are not always augmented by motor behavior; MLI gating of supralinear climbing fiber Ca2+ signaling may prevent unwarranted adaptation during accurately performed movements.
results.evaluation: Claims C63 and C68 represent key conceptual conclusions of the study. C63 is directly supported by the in vivo imaging data, while C68 is a well-reasoned inference about the functional significance of MLI gating based on the experimental findings.

results.result: Expert mice reliably performed cued licking with increased PC Ca2+ event frequency at licking onset; parallel fiber and MLI Ca2+ activity closely tracked lick rate and showed close correspondence during licking.
results.evaluation: Claims C19, C20, C21, and C24 are supported by behavioral and imaging data (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). These claims establish the behavioral context and confirm parallel fiber and MLI activation during the motor task.

results.result: GCaMP6f is sensitive enough to report slight alterations in PC Ca2+ signals evoked by unexpected sensory stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claim C23 is supported by citation to prior work (Najafi et al., 2014b) and addresses a potential concern about indicator sensitivity. This validates the use of GCaMP6f for detecting changes in Ca2+ signal amplitude.

results.result: Bilateral chemogenetic suppression of MLIs in Crus II slows licking rate.
results.evaluation: Claim C30 is supported by citation to prior work (Gaffield and Christie, 2017) and provides context for why unilateral manipulation was used in the current study to avoid behavioral confounds.

results.result: Climbing fiber Ca2+ activity increases at the onset of water consumption; external sensory cues that guide associative learning evoke graded climbing fiber Ca2+ signals in PC dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claims C64 and C65 are supported by citations to prior work and provide context for interpreting when climbing fiber Ca2+ signals might be enhanced during behavior, particularly during learning versus practiced movements.

results.result: Spike bursting of granule cells could shift the balance of parallel fiber excitation and feed-forward inhibition through short-term plasticity; MLIs inhibit one another through GABAergic interconnections.
results.evaluation: Claims C66 and C67 are supported by citations to prior work and represent speculative mechanisms by which the balance of excitation and inhibition might be altered during learning. These are reasonable hypotheses for future investigation.
